title: Zee Just Bought the FIFA World Cup. Ten Days Before Kickoff. For a Third of What FIFA Wanted.
excerpt: After months of standoff, Zee Entertainment secures India broadcast rights for the 2026 World Cup and 38 other FIFA events through 2034, launching a new sports network called Unite8. Here's what it means for fans in India and abroad.
body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off on June 11 in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Until yesterday, nobody in India knew where they'd watch it.

Now they do. Zee Entertainment announced on June 1 that it has secured the broadcast and streaming rights for the World Cup and 38 other FIFA events through 2034. The deal ends what had become an increasingly awkward months-long standoff that left one of the world's largest football-watching populations without a confirmed broadcaster just days before the tournament began.

## The Price Tag

FIFA originally wanted roughly $100 million for the India package covering the 2026 and 2030 World Cups. JioStar, the Reliance-Disney joint venture that aired the 2022 World Cup through its predecessor Viacom18, offered approximately $20 million. FIFA rejected it. Sony, which held rights for the 2014 and 2018 tournaments, discussed a bid but ultimately didn't submit one.

Zee stepped in and reportedly paid around $60 million — significantly less than FIFA's initial ask but three times what JioStar offered. For Zee, it's a strategic re-entry into sports broadcasting roughly eight years after selling its previous sports assets to Sony.

## Unite8 Sports

To house the World Cup and future FIFA properties, Zee is launching an entirely new sports network: Unite8 Sports. Four dedicated channels will go live — Unite8 Sports 1 and Unite8 Sports 1 HD in Hindi, Unite8 Sports 2 and Unite8 Sports 2 HD in English. Digital streaming will be available on ZEE5.

Airtel Digital TV has already lined up the four channels in the 300-303 band, starting June 4. The branding has gone live on Instagram. It's a remarkably fast rollout for a brand that didn't exist a week ago.

The name "Unite8" carries obvious symbolism — eight letters, eight years of rights, a nod to football's unifying power. Whether the branding sticks with Indian audiences remains to be seen, but the content behind it is undeniable.

## What This Covers

This isn't just a World Cup deal. The eight-year partnership includes the 2026 and 2030 men's World Cups, the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, men's and women's U-17 and U-20 World Cups across multiple cycles, FIFA Futsal World Cups, the FIFA Intercontinental Cup, and exclusive docu-series content tied to these tournaments.

That's a year-round football content pipeline — something India has never had under a single broadcaster. For a country where football fandom has been growing rapidly but coverage has been fragmented across multiple platforms, the consolidation under one roof could be significant.

## The NRI Angle

For the diaspora, the viewing equation is simpler — the World Cup will be available across American, British, and Canadian networks through their respective broadcasters. But the Zee deal matters for a different reason: your family back home can now watch the same tournament you're watching.

This is the first World Cup hosted entirely in North American time zones. Group stage matches will run between 11 AM and 9 PM Eastern Time, which translates to roughly 8:30 PM to 6:30 AM IST. The late-night and early-morning kickoff times in India mean this will be a uniquely shared experience — NRIs watching in prime time while their parents and siblings in Delhi or Mumbai set alarms for 1:30 AM matches.

Zee's availability on ZEE5 means streaming access should work globally, though geo-restrictions and regional licensing could complicate matters depending on which country you're in.

## The Bigger Picture

Zee's move is as much about survival as it is about sports. The company has been navigating a turbulent period following the collapse of its proposed merger with Sony Pictures Networks India. Securing a marquee global sports property gives Zee something it desperately needs: relevance among younger audiences who have been migrating to JioStar and other platforms.

Punit Goenka, Zee's CEO, framed it in characteristically corporate terms: "Football cuts across regions and demographics, and the investments in garnering the media rights and launching dedicated sports channels reflect our clear belief in its long-term potential."

Translation: we needed a big swing, and this was the biggest available.

## The Countdown

Ten days. That's all the time Zee has to build awareness, onboard advertisers, ensure technical infrastructure across four new channels and a streaming platform, and convince roughly 1.4 billion people that Unite8 Sports is where they should be when the opening whistle blows on June 11.

It's a sprint. But for Indian football fans who were genuinely worried they might miss the World Cup entirely, the relief is palpable. The broadcast question is settled. Now they just need to figure out the alarm clock.
